titleStmt.title: History of the Zhou Dynasty · Shang 商

div.head: c. 1260 BC
div.p: After Pan Geng's death his younger brothers Xiao Xin and Xiao Yi succeeded in turn; by the accession of Xiao Yi's son Wu Ding, the Middle Shang culture had formally passed into Yinxu Phase I.

The main body of the Zhukaigou people left the Ordos region and moved south into northern Shaanxi, exerting a certain influence on the Shang culture of the Guanzhong region; the characteristic Zhukaigou vessel, the snake-pattern li, has been unearthed at Shang-culture sites such as Beicun in Yao County and Yijiabu in Fufeng. Some scholars take them to be the Fang.

During Wu Ding's reign a series of campaigns was also made against the fang states and tribes of the Wei River valley; since the Middle Shang the Shang culture of Guanzhong had taken on an ever more local character, and Wu Ding's dispatch of armies against the Quanfang may be an epitome of the Shang court's attempt to tighten its hold on the western lands once more.

The "Zhoufang" of the oracle-bone inscriptions is generally taken to be the Zhou people who later founded the Zhou dynasty. In the earlier part of King Wu Ding's reign, corresponding in archaeological terms to Yinxu Phase I, the Zhengjiapo culture appeared in the valley of the Qishui River, its sites interspersed with those of the Jingdang-type Shang culture of the Zhouyuan region. At the same time the Sunjia type appeared around Binzhou and Xunyi, close in its cultural character to the Zhengjiapo culture; both have been regarded by scholars as Proto-Zhou culture.

div.head: c. 1260–1235 BC
div.p: The oracle-bone inscriptions show that King Wu Ding of Shang, in the early part of his reign, conquered one after another the Gengfang, Fou, the Jifang, the Jianfang and other states, and gained control of the southern Shanxi region.

Archaeology shows that with the Late Shang Yinxu Phase I the indigenous cultural elements at the Shijia site in Huantai were replaced by Shang culture; the Yinxu oracle-bone inscriptions have a member of the royal clan called Zi Hua, enfeoffed in the east in Wu Ding's first years, whose fief was likewise called Hua. Some scholars hold that Zi Hua was enfeoffed to guard the land the Shang court had newly conquered.

After his campaigns against the fang states of southern Shanxi, Wu Ding went on, with Que, to campaign against the Zhifang and the Peifang; by the inscriptions' description of their position, both bordered the Qiongfang. Yue rose in revolt early in Wu Ding's reign and was likewise put down by Que. After the Zhifang was conquered by the Shang court, its chief Zhi Guo became Wu Ding's vassal, guarding the western frontier for him, sending troops to help him attack the Bafang, and putting down the revolt of the state of Tan in the east.

After this Wu Ding raised a great army and defeated the Qiongfang's ally, the Tufang. Wu Ding's consort Fu Zi was one of the commanders of the campaign against the Tufang; the oracle-bone inscriptions record "calling on Fu Zi to attack the Tufang". Fu Zi is also recorded, in the early part of Wu Ding's reign, as campaigning against the Yifang, the Bafang and other states. Another consort of Wu Ding, Fu Geng, also went out against the Longfang.

Of the fang states that raided the Shang, most raided at widely scattered points but on a small scale each time; not so the Qiongfang, whose raids were frequent and highly destructive, and which often joined with the Tufang to its east in attacking the Shang court. Some scholars connect the Qiongfang with the remains of the Shilou type in archaeological terms, which may have some bearing on its steady extension of its power into the central Shanxi region from the Middle Shang period onward.

After defeating the Tufang, Wu Ding opened his offensive against the Qiongfang; but Fu Zi does not appear in the inscriptions recording that campaign, and some scholars conclude from this that she died after the campaign against the Tufang and before that against the Qiongfang.

On the archaeological level, in Yinxu Phase I the Shang culture of the Han River region was fading away, yet bronze metals from the south still flowed in quantity into the centre of Yin Shang rule, which shows that the Shang court was still at pains to keep indirect control over the peoples of the south; to secure the "copper road", Wu Ding in his reign launched a southern expedition and attacked the Hufang and the Moufang. The Yinxu Phase I inscriptions record Wu Ding and Wang Cheng campaigning against the Moufang, which thereafter appears no more in the inscriptions and is presumed to have been destroyed.

div.head: c. 1260–1235 BC: archaeological appearances
div.p: The Weiyingzi culture developed in succession to the Lower Xiajiadian culture.
The Weifang Phase III culture developed into the Weifang type.

The Miaotaizi type arose; it, the Dachengdun type, the Wucheng culture and other cultures have each been taken by different scholars to be the Hufang. The Lujiahe culture, the Shidiba culture and the Zhouliangyuqiao culture arose.

div.head: c. 1235 BC
div.p: Late Shang culture entered Yinxu Phase II, whose early stage corresponds roughly to the middle and later part of Wu Ding's reign.

From Yinxu Phase II the Liujia culture, regarded by many scholars as the "Qiangfang culture", began a strong rise; its people moved east into the Zhouyuan region, hastening the decline of the Jingdang-type Shang culture.

The Lijiaya culture and the Xicha culture arose; some scholars, from the record in the Zhouyi and the pottery inscriptions unearthed at the Lijiaya site in Qingjian, infer that the Guifang may be the Lijiaya culture.
The Dachengdun type of Late Shang culture gradually went into decline and died out after Pan Geng's move to Yin; the Dachengdun Phase IV culture arose.
As the Weiyingzi culture developed, the Xiaobaiyang type took shape within it.
The Wucheng culture took over from the Shihuishan culture and carried its development forward.

div.head: c. 1230–1150 BC
div.p: The Shang court's war against the Qiongfang went on by fits and starts and dragged out over many years; down to the last years of Wu Ding's reign there are still inscriptions divining about "capturing the Qiongfang" and the like, after which it is no longer seen in the inscriptional record. On the archaeological side, the material remains of the Shilou type suffered heavy damage in Yinxu Phase II: the large rammed-earth buildings at the Gaohong site in Liulin were abandoned, and the type shows a state of decline. These phenomena, it seems, can be connected with Wu Ding's campaigns against the Qiongfang.

After Yinxu Phase II a number of aristocratic tombs of Shang culture, of fairly high rank, appeared in the central Shanxi region; among them, the inscriptions on the bronzes from the Shang tombs at Jingjie in Lingshi and Qiaobei in Fushan have been shown on analysis to belong to the states of Bing and Xian, under the Shang king. Some scholars hold that the Shang king enfeoffed the two states of Bing and Xian to secure the fruits of the victory over the Qiongfang and so keep the north-west stable.

The Heir Apparent Xiao Ji died before Wu Ding. In the texts of the Warring States period he is described as the model of a filial son, and texts from the Han onward enriched the story of Xiao Ji further. On the archaeological side, Xiao Ji is called the "Junior King" in the inscriptions of the early and middle part of Wu Ding's reign; in the late part of Wu Ding's reign Xiao Ji died, a day name was added to his style, and in sacrifice he is called "Junior King Ji".

According to the transmitted texts, Wu Ding was on the throne for as long as fifty-nine years. In his last years Wu Ding prepared to make his youngest son Zu Jia his successor; but Zu Jia held that his elder brother Zu Geng ought by right to succeed, and so, going against his father's command, he fled and hid among the people.

After Wu Ding's death Zu Geng succeeded to the throne without difficulty; he reigned seven years and at his death passed the throne to Zu Jia. In modern times scholars, by ordering and analysing the oracle-bone inscriptions from Yinxu, have found that Zu Jia carried out a series of reforms in his reign, such as establishing the cyclical sacrifice system, simplifying the sacrificial canon and reducing the number of diviners, which strengthened the royal power and secured the political stability of the Shang court.
In the late stage of Yinxu Phase II, Shang culture for the most part withdrew from the western Guanzhong.

div.head: c. 1230–1150 BC: archaeological appearances
div.p: The Misa-ri type reached its lower limit; central-western South Korea entered the stage of Garak-dong, Heunam-ri and Yeoksam-dong. At the same time the Beomui-guseok Phase II culture arose.
The Xujianian site of the Siwa culture appeared.

div.head: c. 1150 BC
div.p: After Zu Jia's death his sons Lin Xin and Kang Ding succeeded in turn. Unlike the relatively peaceful time of Zu Jia, inscriptions concerned with war became frequent again under Lin Xin and Kang Ding. By the accession of Zu Jia's son Lin Xin, the ever-growing Qiangfang had begun to pose a serious threat to the western lands of the Shang court; with the strong eastward advance of the Liujia culture, not only did Shang culture withdraw from the western Guanzhong, but the Zhengjiapo culture, which had only just begun to gather momentum, was hit as well.

Archaeology shows that at the turn from Yinxu Phase II to Phase III, elements of the late Zhukaigou culture and the Lijiaya culture spread south and, blending with the cultures of Guanzhong, formed the remains of the Zaoshugounao type and the Heidouzui type in the Chunhua region. Some scholars think this may be connected with the Fang, grown strong once more in the inscriptions of Lin Xin and Kang Ding; in the inscriptions of Zu Jia's time what concerns war is very little, yet nearly all of it has to do with the raids of the Fang. By the reigns of Lin Xin and Kang Ding its raids, too, had grown more frequent. Other scholars propose to identify it with the "Xunyu Rong and Di" of the transmitted texts, who forced King Tai of Zhou to move south from Bin to Qi Zhou.
The Qinghai Bronze culture entered the late stage of its middle period; the Upper Zhangjiayuan culture arose.
